reason: Under Differences between SCPs and RCPs the two quotes say SCPs are principal-centric and limit maximum permissions of principals in member accounts, and RCPs are resource-centric and limit maximum permissions for resources in member accounts.
The quote says SCPs and RCPs are independent controls, you can enable only one or both, and using both creates a data perimeter around identities and resources.

The claim is supported, but the value display 'don't attach SCPs to the root' drops the quote's condition 'without thoroughly testing the impact', and qualifiers.condition is empty, so a fact link would teach an absolute rule the quote does not state.

The quote says users and roles must still be granted IAM permission policies and a user without any has no access even if the SCPs allow all services and actions; the context scopes SCPs to member accounts.

Under the Security Tooling (Audit) account heading the quotes give centralized delegated admin access to security tooling, view-only investigative access into all accounts, and the listed aggregated services ('such as' covers the omitted AppConfig).

The quote says limiting sensitive data stores to dedicated accounts lets you control access more tightly and restrict permissions at the coarse-grained account level instead of fine-grained access in a single broad account.

The quote says separate non-production and production accounts separate, by default, a workload environment's resources and data; the heading and preceding sentence give the distinct security and operational controls purpose.

The quote recommends a single organization for all accounts and calls an organization a security boundary that maintains consistency across accounts; the context names policies and service-level configurations.

The quotes say accounts can be created programmatically and provisioned with recommended resources and permissions via CloudFormation StackSets, including per group of development and production accounts.

The quote says a tag policy can enforce noncompliant tagging operations on specified resource types, so those requests are prevented from completing; the claim keeps the specified-resource-type condition.
The quotes say tag policies standardize tags on resources in the organization's accounts and untagged resources or tags not defined in the policy are not evaluated for compliance.
Under Maximum and minimum values the Limit column gives 50 for the number of tags you can attach to a root, OU, or account; scope and maximum match.

The quote says trusted access lets the trusted service perform tasks in the organization and its accounts on your behalf, does not otherwise affect user or role permissions, and the service can create a service-linked role in accounts when needed.

SEC01-BP02 quotes say the root user is the most privileged user and in some cases cannot be constrained by security policies, and to prioritize the management account root user, with preventative controls possible on member account root users.
The two quotes from the RCP page note say use an SCP to limit IAM principals within member accounts and an RCP to restrict external IAM principals requesting access to resources in member accounts.

The quotes support the default loss of access, but RetainSharingOnAccountLeaveOrganization applies only to account-to-account shares (not OU or organization shares, per context) and requires allowExternalPrincipals; the claim's 'unless the share was created with' drops the account-to-account condition.

The quotes say AZs are mapped randomly to names per account, an AZ ID such as use1-az1 is the same physical location in every account, and a subnet shared in use1-az2 is available in the consumer AZ whose ID is also use1-az2.
The quote says only your own organization and its OUs can be added, outside OUs or organizations cannot, and outside individual accounts or, for supported services, IAM roles and users can be added.

Under the Default limit header the row gives 1,500 customer managed permissions; the page intro (checked with show) says these are limits of your AWS account and some can be increased via Support.
The quote says disabling trusted access to Organizations removes principals within the organization from all resource shares and they lose access to the shared resources.

The quotes say sharing must be enabled from the RAM console or enable-sharing-with-aws-organization so the service-linked role is created, and enabling from the Organizations console does not create it and blocks sharing within the organization.
The FAQ quote says AWS managed permissions are created and maintained by AWS and every resource type has a default AWS managed permission.
The FAQ quote says you can specify IAM policies to control access to resources shared with you.
The FAQ quote limits sharing with IAM roles and IAM users to supported resource types, which is what the claim states.
The FAQ quote says all RAM API calls are logged in CloudTrail and CloudWatch Events are triggered whenever resource shares change.
Under the Billing question the FAQ answers that you can share resources at no additional cost.
The FAQ quote says a managed permission defines actions, conditions and principals, and you associate either an AWS managed or a customer managed permission with each resource type in a share.
The FAQ quote lists adding resources to a share, choosing a managed permission for each resource type, and specifying who gets access.
The FAQ quote says you can share with any AWS account and, when in an organization with sharing enabled, with OUs or the entire organization.
The FAQ quote says shared resources also appear in the resource console pages and List/Describe APIs; the context example shows them alongside the account's own rules.
The FAQ quote says you can stop sharing by removing the resource from the share or by deleting the share.
The quotes say RAM uses the managed permission to generate a resource-based policy attached to each shared resource, and the effect of a managed permission is always Allow.
